Organization Mission
The Centre’s mission is to support the long-term evolution of community housing providers by dispensing funds, support and help to increase organizational capacity. To drive transformation, growth, resilience, sustainability and inclusiveness in the community housing sector, the Centre offers support in two forms:

Project Summary 
The Centre lacks a formal Project Management Office (PMO) despite managing numerous projects. This initiative proposes the establishment of a PMO to streamline operations, improve efficiency, and enhance project success. The project aims to introduce standardized project management practices to enhance the planning, execution, and monitoring of various projects. This initiative will establish a framework for consistency, efficiency, and effectiveness in project delivery, ensuring alignment with the Centre's strategic objectives. By instituting best practices, governance, and methodologies, the PMO will enable better resource allocation, risk management, and stakeholder engagement, thereby supporting the Centre's mission to innovate and strengthen community housing through technical assistance and funding grants, ultimately leading to more impactful and sustainable outcomes.
Project Objectives 
The Creation of a Project Management Office (PMO) to oversee all projects coordinated by Community Housing Transformation Centre that will focus on the following procedures:
•	Optimize the allocation and utilization of resources, including personnel, finances, and time, to maximize project outcomes.
•	Improve the planning, execution, and delivery of projects, leading to higher success rates and better alignment with the Centre’s strategic goals.
•	Ensure all projects are aligned with the Centre’s mission and strategic objectives, focusing on transformation, growth, and resilience in the community housing sector.

Location: Port-au-Prince
Country: Haiti

Job Details

Job Posting Organization:
The job posting organization is UNOPS (United Nations Office for Project Services), which was established to help the United Nations and its partners provide peace and Security, Humanitarian Assistance, and sustainable development. UNOPS operates in over 80 countries and has a workforce of more than 20,000 personnel. The organization focuses on project management, infrastructure, and procurement services, ensuring that projects are delivered efficiently and effectively, with a strong emphasis on sustainability and Capacity Building.

Job Overview:
The Project Manager position is crucial for overseeing the successful delivery of projects within the UNOPS framework. The role involves developing and implementing project plans, ensuring that all activities align with the strategic objectives of the organization. The Project Manager will be responsible for managing resources, timelines, and stakeholder engagement, while also ensuring compliance with organizational policies and quality standards. This position requires a proactive approach to identifying risks and opportunities, as well as a commitment to fostering collaboration among team members and stakeholders. The Project Manager will also play a key role in Knowledge Management and innovation, contributing to the continuous improvement of project management practices within UNOPS.

When it comes to launching new products or initiatives, the board of directors may create a steering committee from within the organization or seek outside experts to manage the process. A steering committee plays an imperative role in the success of projects and initiatives. To enable success, the steering committee needs to host productive committee meetings. Read on to learn more about steering committees and how meeting management software increases their efficiency and effectiveness.

What is a Steering Committee?

A steering committee is a group of individuals, ideally from diverse backgrounds, who are tasked with overseeing large-scale projects, programs, or organizational initiatives. Typically composed of senior leaders and subject matter experts, these committees ensure projects align with organizational goals. Steering committees are crucial because they help bridge the gap between project teams and upper management, ensuring resources are allocated appropriately, timelines are met, and risks are managed effectively.

Board Meeting

Ensure effective, efficient meetings with our comprehensive Board Meeting Agenda Template.

Roles and Responsibilities of a Steering Committee

The roles and responsibilities of a steering committee include the following: 

Provide Advice and Direction

Steering committees offer advice and direction to ensure projects stay aligned with strategic plans. They review progress regularly, helping to identify areas of improvement. Additionally, steering committees offer recommendations on resource allocation, timelines, and stakeholder engagement, essentially becoming a project manager for important tasks.

Set Project Timeline and Budget

Steering committees establish project timeliness by aligning project milestones with strategic objectives and resource availability. They also allocate budgets based on cost projections and risk assessments. 

By setting clear expectations and milestones, the committee ensures all stakeholders are aligned and accountable for meeting deadlines and staying within budgetary constraints. This financial oversight helps minimize risks and fosters a sense of responsibility among team members. 

Monitor Project Quality

To ensure outcomes meet the standards of the organization’s and stakeholders’ goals, steering committees must successfully monitor the project’s quality. By implementing quality control measures, the committee can identify any issues early in the process and take corrective action, ultimately ensuring the project’s success.

Evaluate and Monitor Risk

Steering committees are tasked with identifying potential risks that could impede project progress. This includes assessing internal and external factors that may affect timelines, budgets, and outcomes. 

In collaboration with the risk committee, a steering committee works proactively to develop risk mitigation strategies, ensuring contingency plans are in place to address unforeseen challenges. This vigilance not only helps safeguard the project but also fosters a culture of resilience within the organization.

Advocacy Director Salary & Outlook

An Advocacy Director’s salary is influenced by the organization’s size and funding, the complexity of issues addressed, years of experience in advocacy or related fields, and the success record in policy change or campaign achievements. Additionally, negotiation skills and existing networks within relevant political or social spheres can significantly impact compensation.

  • Median Annual Salary: $110,250 ($53/hour)
  • Top 10% Annual Salary: $200,000 ($96.15/hour)

The employment of advocacy directors is expected to grow much faster than average over the next decade.

This surge is driven by increasing societal focus on social justice, environmental concerns, and public health issues, necessitating organizations to engage more actively in policy advocacy, public relations, and stakeholder engagement, thereby elevating the demand for skilled Advocacy Directors to lead these complex initiatives.

Advocacy Director Job Requirements

Education: An Advocacy Director typically holds a Bachelor’s or Master’s Degree, often in fields like Political Science, Public Administration, Communications, or Social Work. Coursework emphasizing critical thinking, public policy, advocacy strategies, and effective communication is crucial. A strong academic foundation in research methods, ethics, and leadership also supports the multifaceted responsibilities of this role. Advanced degrees may offer specialized knowledge in policy analysis, nonprofit management, or legal frameworks, enhancing the director’s ability to lead impactful advocacy campaigns.

Experience: Advocacy Directors typically emerge from a diverse background of professional experiences, often rooted in roles that demand strong leadership, strategic communication, and policy analysis skills. Their journey often includes significant exposure to public affairs, community organizing, or legal advocacy, where they’ve honed their ability to influence public opinion and policy. On-the-job training and participation in specialized training programs are common, equipping them with the tools to effectively manage campaigns, engage stakeholders, and navigate the complexities of nonprofit, governmental, or corporate environments. This role demands a blend of practical experience in advocacy, coupled with a track record of successful team leadership and project management.

Meet our Speakers:

About the Session:

In California, digital transformation is revolutionizing public infrastructure projects, driving efficiency enhancements and elevating service standards. The state is at the forefront of adopting cutting-edge technologies like the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and cloud computing to bolster connectivity, intelligence, and data-driven decision-making in infrastructure systems. Examples include IoT sensors for real-time monitoring on vital highways, AI algorithms optimizing traffic flow in major cities like Los Angeles and San Francisco, and cloud-based platforms enabling predictive maintenance in critical infrastructure projects. Moreover, digital platforms and mobile applications are pivotal, enhancing communication and stakeholder engagement, thereby facilitating seamless project management. These advancements yield streamlined operations, cost reductions, and improved service delivery across sectors, benefiting both Californian residents and businesses.

Power project in Kenya, for example, is the largest of its kind in Africa. It achieved financial close through a diverse mix of funding that included development finance institutions and private sector equity. This resilient infrastructure endeavor highlights how project finance can be leveraged even in challenging environments.

Moving to India, the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation stands as a paradigm of efficacious project finance. The project’s success lies in its comprehensive planning and execution, involving international development banks and public-private partnerships. With over 390 km of operational network, the Delhi Metro illustrates how infrastructure financing can be managed effectively to create a public transport revolution in a densely populated urban area.

Challenges and Opportunities in Latin America

Latin America, with countries like Brazil and Mexico, presents a mixed scenario of challenges and opportunities. In Brazil, the Belo Monte Hydroelectric Plant is a testament to the ability of project finance to underpin massive infrastructure developments. However, the project also faced environmental and social concerns, underlining the complexity of deploying large-scale infrastructure in sensitive areas.

Mexico’s projects, such as the New Mexico International Airport, have been hindered by political and policy unpredictability, impeding long-term infrastructure investment. Yet, these challenges also highlight the opportunities for mitigating risks through enhanced due diligence and stakeholder engagement, thereby improving the investment climate for future endeavors.

Frequently Asked Questions

This section addresses common inquiries regarding the financing of infrastructure projects in emerging economies, with a focus on the sources, impact of climate finance initiatives, roles of international financial institutions, and mobilization of private sector investments.

What are the main sources of funding for infrastructure projects in emerging economies?

The main sources of funding for infrastructure in emerging economies include public finance, concessional finance, private sector investments, and international development finance from entities such as the World Bank. These sources often provide the substantial capital needed for large-scale projects in sectors such as transportation, energy, and water.

How do climate finance initiatives impact infrastructure funding in developing countries?

Climate finance initiatives, by offering financial support for adaptation and mitigation efforts, influence infrastructure funding in developing countries. This evolution from Waterfall to Agile, DevOps, and beyond signifies not just a shift in tools and techniques but a fundamental change in mindset towards collaboration, efficiency, and customer-centric development. Understanding this evolution offers critical insights into current practices and future trends.

From Waterfall to Agile: The Waterfall model, characterized by its sequential, linear progression through the phases of conception, initiation, analysis, design, construction, testing, deployment, and maintenance, dominated the early years of software development. Its structured approach appealed to industries accustomed to predictability and detailed planning. However, the Waterfall model's rigidity became a liability in the face of changing requirements and faster-paced markets. It struggled with flexibility, leading to delays, cost overruns, and often products that were outdated by the time they reached the market.

The Agile methodology emerged as a response to the limitations of the Waterfall model, advocating for iterative development, where requirements and solutions evolve through the collaborative effort of self-organizing and cross-functional teams. Agile focuses on customer involvement, adaptability, and working software over comprehensive documentation, promoting a more dynamic and responsive development environment. This shift significantly impacted project management, emphasizing flexibility, continuous improvement, and stakeholder engagement, thereby enhancing team dynamics with a focus on transparency, communication, and collaboration.

The Rise of DevOps: DevOps arose from the need to unify software development (Dev) and software operation (Ops), addressing gaps left by Agile in continuous delivery and integration. It emphasizes automation, monitoring, and collaboration between developers, QA, and IT operations to improve the speed and quality of software delivery. DevOps further transformed project management by fostering a culture of shared responsibility, continuous feedback, and rapid iteration, challenging traditional roles and silos within teams.

Beyond DevOps - Toward Continuous Improvement: As the industry moves beyond DevOps, we are witnessing the emergence of methodologies that prioritize continuous improvement and adaptability. Concepts like DevSecOps integrate security into the DevOps process, while GitOps and NoOps focus on automation and minimizing human intervention in operations. These evolutions reflect a broader trend towards efficiency, resilience, and security in software development, driven by cloud computing, AI, and other technological advancements.

Factors Driving Changes: Several key factors have driven the evolution of development methodologies. Technological advancements have enabled more complex systems and faster development cycles. PPGIS is defined as the combination of technology-based spatial analysis from GIS and public participation approaches central to collaborative-, community-, and participatory-based processes that provide multiple means to interpret complex data. PPGIS methods usually follow a three-phase process (Craig et al. 2002): (1) identifying existing data (problem identification, gathering or collecting spatial data, generating a geospatial database); (2) data collection and analysis (developing a participatory mapping approach, interviewing/surveying participants, conducting the mapping exercise); and (3) communication of results (integrating qualitative and quantitative data, developing appropriate data outputs). In some instances, the process has been adapted to be both more iterative and reflexive to better bridge the divide between the qualitative and quantitative (Kyttä et al. 2013; Babelon et al. 2017).

PPGIS has been used in a range of contexts such as protected area management, national forest planning, mapping ecosystems services, and community urban development studies (Brown and Kyttä 2014). These contexts are centred around the benefit of public involvement and participation activities to improve equity of access and stakeholder engagement, thereby reducing conflict, increasing representation, and increasing community buy-in for controversial planning proposals (Schlossberg and Shuford 2005). For example, the method has been used to highlight the differences in perceptions and knowledge of mangroves and ecotourism to better inform forest conservation strategies (Satyanarayana et al. 2012). PPGIS has also been applied to assessments of cultural ecosystem services across local and national scales, to inform policy around climate change mitigation planning (Jaligot et al. 2019).

However, PPGIS is not without its issues. Public participation GIS often relies on highly technical tools that can limit community engagement, due to unequal access to resources (e.g., computer access and digital literacy) (Robinson et al. 2017). Paper-based “offline” mapping methods can encounter similar barriers, based on a community’s awareness of information sources and their ability to apply the GIS outputs (e.g., Indigenous local knowledge in “resource-poor” communities) (Elwood and Leitner 1998; Benyei et al. 2020).
